title: Utopia
alternative_titles: Libellus vere aureus, nec minus salutaris quam festivus, de optimo rei publicae statu deque nova insula Utopia
description: A humanist dialogue in two books describing the imaginary island commonwealth of Utopia, where property is held in common, religious toleration prevails, and the social and economic abuses of early sixteenth-century Europe are criticized by contrast.
plot_or_argument: Book I frames the work as a report of a conversation in Antwerp among More himself, his friend Peter Giles, and the fictional traveller Raphael Hythlodaeus, who denounces the social evils of Europe — enclosure, penal severity, court flattery — and debates whether a philosopher should serve princes. Book II contains Hythlodaeus's full description of Utopia: its geography, magistrates, working day, communal property, marriage customs, education, religion, and warfare.
narrative_structure: Two-part dialogue framed by a prefatory letter to Peter Giles and paratexts (maps, Utopian alphabet and quatrain); Book I is a debate on counsel, Book II a systematic description of the island, with the whole enclosed in the fiction of Hythlodaeus's eyewitness report.
principal_characters: Thomas More; Peter Giles; Raphael Hythlodaeus; Cardinal John Morton (recalled in the dialogue)
historical_context: Composed in 1515–16 during More's embassy to the Netherlands for the wool trade negotiations, at the height of his humanist circle's activities; printed at Louvain by Thierry Martens under the supervision of Erasmus, Giles, and others, and translated into English by Ralph Robinson in 1551.
literary_significance: The founding text of the utopian genre and one of the masterpieces of northern humanism; its punning title (ou-topia 'no place' / eu-topia 'good place') and its fusion of satire, political theory, and fiction made it the most influential secular prose work of the English Renaissance, directly shaping works from Bacon's New Atlantis to modern dystopian fiction.
bibliographical_notes: First edition Louvain 1516 (Martens); second (Paris, 1517) and third (Basel, Froben, 1518) editions revised by More; first English translation by Ralph Robinson (1551). The standard Latin text is in the Yale Complete Works, vol. 4, ed. Edward Surtz and J. H. Hexter (1965); modern English versions include Paul Turner's Penguin translation (1965, rev. 2003).

title: The History of King Richard III
alternative_titles: History of King Richard the Third
description: More's unfinished prose history of the rise and fall of Richard III, composed in parallel English and Latin versions; the English text was first printed in a corrupt form in Hardyng's Chronicle (1543) and the definitive version appeared in Rastell's edition of More's English Works (1557).
plot_or_argument: The narrative traces Richard's path to the throne: the death of Edward IV, Richard's seizure of power as Protector, the removal of the princes, Buckingham's rebellion, and Richard's coronation and brief reign, breaking off during Morton's embassy to France. It portrays Richard as a dissembling tyrant whose deformity mirrors his moral deformity.
narrative_structure: Unfinished chronicle in five books, driven by dramatic set-piece speeches (Buckingham's oration, Elizabeth Woodville's lament) and a Tacitean focus on character and motive rather than providential design.
principal_characters: Richard III; Edward IV; Elizabeth Woodville; Henry Stafford, Duke of Buckingham; John Morton; Lord Hastings; Edward V; Richard, Duke of York
historical_context: Written during More's second period of public service, probably 1513–1518, drawing on oral testimony from Morton's household where More was raised; the work circulated in manuscript and shaped the Tudor 'black legend' of Richard III long before Shakespeare used Hall's chronicle (which incorporated More's account) for his play.
literary_significance: The first great work of English prose history and the fountainhead of the Tudor myth of Richard III; its psychological portraiture and dramatic irony made it a major source for Shakespeare and for sixteenth-century historiography.
bibliographical_notes: Latin version first printed 1565 (Louvain); the authoritative English text is in The Complete Works of St Thomas More, vol. 2, ed. Richard S. Sylvester (Yale, 1963); paperback: The History of King Richard III, ed. Sylvester (Yale, 1976).

title: A Dialogue Concerning Heresies
alternative_titles: A Dialogue of Sir Thomas More, Knight
description: More's first and longest English polemical work against the Lutheran heresy, cast as a four-book dialogue between More and a young 'messenger' sent by a friend who is tempted by the reformers.
plot_or_argument: In Book I More defends the veneration of images, pilgrimages, and miracles; Book II discusses the authority of the Church and the corruption of Tyndale's New Testament translation; Book III refutes Luther's and Tyndale's views on faith and works; Book IV defends the clergy and the burning of heretics, arguing that Luther's doctrine leads to sedition and the destruction of the sacraments.
narrative_structure: Four books of continuous dialogue; the anonymous messenger relays objections while More answers at length with authorities, anecdotes, and comic deflation of the reformers.
historical_context: Written 1528–29 after More had read Tyndale's New Testament and his Obedience of a Christian Man; part of the print war between More (with Bishop John Fisher) and the English reformers conducted under Bishop Tunstall's licence to read heretical books.
literary_significance: The major English Catholic response to the early Reformation, documenting the doctrinal battle over scripture and tradition, and one of the fullest exhibits of More's prose — combative, witty, and colloquial — outside the Latin works.
bibliographical_notes: First printed by John Rastell, June 1529 (STC 18084); text in The Complete Works of St Thomas More, vol. 6, ed. Thomas M. C. Lawler, Germain Marc'hadour and Richard Marius (Yale, 1981).

title: The Supplication of Souls
description: More's defence of purgatory, written as the answer of the souls in purgatory to Simon Fish's Supplication for the Beggars (1529), which had demanded the dissolution of the monasteries and denounced purgatory as a clerical fiction.
plot_or_argument: The souls of the dead speak in their own persons, showing from scripture and reason that purgatory exists, that prayers and masses for the dead avail them, and that those who deny purgatory rob both the dead and the living poor who depend on clerical charity.
narrative_structure: A continuous oration in two books, framed as a supplication addressed to the king, lords, and commons, with the dead themselves as the petitioners.
historical_context: Printed late in 1529 as a direct reply to Fish's Supplication for the Beggars, which Henry VIII is said to have shown to More; the exchange belongs to the parliamentary debates of the Reformation Parliament and the campaign against church wealth.
literary_significance: The most rhetorically inventive of More's early controversial works — using the fiction of the speaking dead — and a key document of the pre-Reformation debate on purgatory and monastic wealth.
bibliographical_notes: First printed by William Rastell, 1529 (STC 18092); text in The Complete Works of St Thomas More, vol. 7, ed. Frank Manley, Germain Marc'hadour, Richard Marius and Clarence H. Miller (Yale, 1990).

title: A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation
description: More's last and greatest English work, written in the Tower of London while awaiting execution, a dialogue in which an elderly Hungarian uncle instructs his nephew on bearing tribulation, especially the fear of death under persecution.
plot_or_argument: Set in Hungary on the eve of a Turkish invasion, the dialogue moves from the general consolation of tribulation, through the temptations of fear, scruple, and despair, to the specific comfort of martyrdom, culminating in the uncle's meditation on the passion of Christ as the pattern of all suffering.
narrative_structure: Three books of dialogue between the aged Anthony and his nephew Vincent, with inset parables and a famous treatment of the temptation to suicide; the fictional frame thinly veils More's own imprisonment.
historical_context: Written in the Tower between More's arrest (April 1534) and execution (6 July 1535), after his refusal of the Oath of Succession; the manuscript was smuggled abroad and first printed in London by Richard Tottel in 1553, under Mary I.
literary_significance: The masterpiece of English devotional prose of its age, and one of the great prison writings in the language; its controlled serenity under sentence of death has made it the most widely read of More's English works.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1553 (STC 18082); authoritative text in The Complete Works of St Thomas More, vol. 12, ed. Louis L. Martz and Frank Manley (Yale, 1976).

title: Epigrammata
alternative_titles: Epigrammata clarissimi disertissimique viri Thomae Mori
description: More's collected Latin epigrams, printed together with his Utopia in 1518, including translations from the Greek Anthology, satirical and courtly verse, and the poems on his own fortune and on kingship.
plot_or_argument: The collection has no single argument; it ranges from verse translations of Greek epigrams made with William Lily, through witty satires on astrologers and courtiers, to the programmatic 'Progymnasmata' and poems celebrating the accession of Henry VIII.
narrative_structure: A printed miscellany grouped by type: translations from the Greek Anthology, original epigrams, and the coronation poems of 1509.
meter_and_prosody: Elegiac couplets, hendecasyllables, and other classical metres
historical_context: Composed across More's humanist career from the late 1490s; the Progymnasmata with Lily (an exercise translating Greek epigrams) dates from c. 1503–04; the collection was printed by Froben at Basel in 1518 together with the third edition of Utopia.
literary_significance: The finest Latin verse written by an Englishman of the early Renaissance and a showcase of the Erasmian revival of classical epigram; the coronation poems mark the beginnings of English Renaissance panegyric.
bibliographical_notes: Text in The Complete Works of St Thomas More, vol. 3, part 2, ed. Clarence H. Miller, Leicester Bradner, Charles A. Lynch and Revilo P. Oliver (Yale, 1984).

title: The Boke Named the Governour
description: Elyot's treatise on the education and conduct of the English ruling class, the first major work of English political and educational theory written in the vernacular rather than Latin.
plot_or_argument: The first book prescribes the upbringing of a future governor from infancy — nurses, tutors, the curriculum of classical authors, music, painting, and physical exercise. The second book treats the virtues proper to a ruler: justice, fortitude, temperance, wisdom, and the golden mean. The third discusses the cardinal virtues and their application in counsel and judgement.
narrative_structure: Three books of systematic exposition, dense with citation of Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, and Plutarch, and illustrated with exemplary stories of classical princes.
historical_context: Written c. 1530–31 while Elyot, a diplomat and clerk, was out of royal favour after Wolsey's fall; dedicated to Henry VIII, it drew on Castiglione's Il Cortegiano and Patrizi's De regno, and shaped the humanist programme of gentlemanly education institutionalized in the grammar schools.
literary_significance: A founding text of English humanism in the vernacular: it established the ideal of the educated magistrate, coined or first recorded many English words ('education', 'encyclopaedia'), and remained an authority on gentlemanly conduct for two centuries.
bibliographical_notes: First printed by Thomas Berthelet, 1531 (STC 7635); standard modern edition: The Book Named the Governor, ed. S. E. Lehmberg (Everyman, 1962; repr. 1975).

title: The Castle of Health
description: Elyot's vernacular treatise on diet and regimen, the first substantial English medical handbook written by a layman for lay readers.
plot_or_argument: The book surveys the four humours and complexions, the properties of foods and drinks, sleep, exercise, and the regimen proper to each age and season, advising the reader how to preserve health through moderation and self-knowledge.
narrative_structure: Four books of systematic exposition, compiled from Galen, Hippocrates, and the medieval regimen literature.
historical_context: Written in the mid-1530s and printed by Thomas Berthelet in 1539 (with editions to 1610); Elyot's attempt to bring learned medicine into English paralleled his linguistic programme in The Governour.
literary_significance: A landmark in the vernacularization of medicine and natural knowledge in Tudor England, influential on later dietary literature and a document of humanist attitudes to the body.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1539 (STC 7643); facsimile editions: Scholars' Facsimiles & Reprints, 1937. Modern study: The Castel of Helth Corrected and in Some Places Augmented, 1541, ed. S. A. Tannenbaum (1937).

title: The Dictionary
alternative_titles: The Dictionary of Syr Thomas Eliot Knyght
description: Elyot's Latin–English dictionary, the first classical dictionary of the English language and the basis of the later English lexicographical tradition.
plot_or_argument: A reference work with no argument: Latin headwords with English definitions, drawing on Calepino's Dictionarium and enriched by Elyot's own scholarship, published in a revised edition as Bibliotheca Eliotae in 1542 (revised and enlarged by Thomas Cooper, 1548).
narrative_structure: Alphabetical dictionary entries.
historical_context: Compiled 1536–38 for Thomas Berthelet, with a dedication to Henry VIII; it was the first Latin–English dictionary intended for the study of classical authors rather than the medieval vocabularies, and Cooper's revisions made it the foundation of Renaissance lexicography in England.
literary_significance: The founding work of English lexicography: it made classical learning accessible in the vernacular, standardized English equivalents for Latin terms, and served as the model for all subsequent Latin–English dictionaries.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1538 (STC 7659); Bibliotheca Eliotae 1542 (STC 7659.5). Facsimile of the 1538 edition: Scolar Press, 1970.

title: Toxophilus
description: Ascham's dialogue on the art of archery, presented to Henry VIII as both a practical treatise and a model of English prose style — the first book on a sport written in the English language.
plot_or_argument: Two speakers, Toxophilus ('lover of the bow') and Philologus ('lover of learning'), debate whether study or shooting better befits a gentleman; Toxophilus vindicates archery as recreation, describes the bow, its parts, and the craft of shooting, and argues for the health and military value of the sport, while the dialogue itself demonstrates the eloquence the English tongue can achieve.
narrative_structure: Two-book dialogue framed by a preface to 'all gentle men and yeomen of England', with a systematic technical exposition embedded in the conversational form.
historical_context: Written 1544–45 when Ascham was reader in Greek at St John's College, Cambridge, and presented to Henry VIII in 1545 in the royal library at Westminster, for which Ascham received a pension; archery's military role had been reaffirmed by statute in 1541.
literary_significance: The first English treatise on a sport and a deliberate demonstration of the capacities of English prose for learned subjects; together with The Schoolmaster it established Ascham's reputation as a stylist and educational theorist.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1545 (STC 837); standard edition: Toxophilus: The School of Shooting, ed. Giles E. Dawson (Cambridge, 1904); also in Ascham's English Works, ed. W. A. Wright (Cambridge, 1904).

title: The Schoolmaster
description: Ascham's posthumously published treatise on the education of children, especially the teaching of Latin by double translation, with an autobiographical preface on the occasion of its writing.
plot_or_argument: Book I, framed by the preface recalling a 1563 dinner conversation at Windsor on the flogging of schoolboys, advocates gentleness in teaching, criticizes the harsh grammar-school regime, and sketches the ideal education of a gentleman's son. Book II offers a practical method — the 'double translation' of Latin — by which the student imitates classical models, with detailed advice on style, imitation, and the choice of authors.
narrative_structure: Two books; the first is anecdotal and hortatory, the second a systematic method with specimen exercises.
principal_characters: Roger Ascham (narrator); Sir William Cecil; Sir Richard Sackville
historical_context: Begun c. 1563 after the Windsor dinner with Cecil and Sackville (the latter of whom prompted the book), and left unfinished at Ascham's death in December 1568; published in 1570 by his widow Margaret with a dedication to Cecil. Its composition and publication bridge the early Tudor and Elizabethan periods.
literary_significance: The classic statement of Elizabethan humanist pedagogy; its doctrine of imitation and its advocacy of the vernacular prose style influenced Sidney, Spenser, and the school curriculum for generations.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1570 (STC 832); standard edition: The Schoolmaster (1570), ed. Lawrence V. Ryan (Cornell University Press for the Folger Shakespeare Library, 1967).

title: The Life of Sir Thomas More
alternative_titles: The Lyfe of Sir Thomas Moore, Knighte
description: William Roper's intimate biography of his father-in-law Sir Thomas More, written in the 1550s but not printed until 1626; the first biography in English of a private subject written by a close contemporary.
plot_or_argument: Roper recounts More's household and public career from his own memory and family tradition: More's early marriage and life at Chelsea, his rise under Henry VIII, the succession crisis, his resignation of the chancellorship, his imprisonment, trial, and execution, with the celebrated dialogues between More and his wife and daughters and More's reported words to his son-in-law on the king's favour.
narrative_structure: A continuous first-person memoir in chronological order, emphasizing the domestic and moral More, with set-piece conversations and the famous 'King's servant but God's first' speech.
principal_characters: Sir Thomas More; William Roper (narrator); Margaret Roper (More's daughter); Alice More; Henry VIII
historical_context: Written c. 1553–58, probably during Mary's reign, by More's son-in-law who had lived in More's household for sixteen years; circulated in manuscript (the 'Harpsfield' manuscript) and first printed at Saint-Omer in 1626, with the first English printing in 1726.
literary_significance: The founding text of English biographical writing and the principal source for the domestic life of More; its vivid remembered dialogue made it one of the most influential portraits of a Tudor statesman ever written.
bibliographical_notes: First printed (Saint-Omer) 1626; standard edition: The Life of Sir Thomas More, in Two Early Tudor Lives, ed. Richard S. Sylvester and Davis P. Harding (Yale, 1962).

title: The Life and Death of Cardinal Wolsey
description: George Cavendish's memoir of Cardinal Wolsey, composed in the 1550s from the author's service in Wolsey's household; the first major English biography written by a layman and household servant.
plot_or_argument: Cavendish recounts Wolsey's rise from butcher's son to cardinal and lord chancellor, his magnificence and building, the divorce crisis and the legatine court, his fall from favour, his death at Leicester Abbey in 1530, and the moral of Fortune's wheel; the narrative is thick with eyewitness detail of the cardinal's household, progresses, and final days.
narrative_structure: A first-person memoir in chronological order, framed by a prologue on Fortune and divided by the rise, greatness, and fall of its subject; interludes of verse mark the turns of fortune.
principal_characters: Cardinal Thomas Wolsey; George Cavendish (narrator); Henry VIII; Anne Boleyn; Thomas Cromwell (in the final scenes)
historical_context: Written c. 1554–58, partly to vindicate Wolsey against the Protestant chroniclers Hall and Foxe; circulated in manuscript for decades and used by Stow, Holinshed, and Shakespeare, before its first printing in 1641 as The Negotiations of Thomas Wolsey.
literary_significance: A masterpiece of Tudor biographical prose and the great contemporary portrait of Wolsey; its sympathetic account of the cardinal's fall and its influence on Shakespeare's Henry VIII make it a central document of early English biography.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1641 (Wing C1619); standard edition: The Life and Death of Cardinal Wolsey, in Two Early Tudor Lives, ed. Richard S. Sylvester and Davis P. Harding (Yale, 1962).

title: A Treatise of Moral Philosophy
alternative_titles: A Treatise of Morall Phylosophie, Contaynyng the Sayinges of the Wyse
description: William Baldwin's popular compilation of moral sayings and exemplary lives of philosophers, first published by Edward Whitchurch in 1547 and enlarged by Thomas Palfreyman; one of the most frequently reprinted English books of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
plot_or_argument: The book arranges the sayings of the ancient philosophers under topical heads — of God, of wisdom, of justice, of friendship — and follows them with brief lives of the philosophers, ending each section with moral application for Christian readers.
narrative_structure: A compendium in four books: sayings of the philosophers, their lives, answers and apophthegms, and parables, with a running apparatus of moralization.
historical_context: Compiled in the 1540s by Baldwin, then a corrector in Edward Whitchurch's printing house, during the flood of popular moral and sententious literature under Edward VI; Palfreyman's enlarged version (1555 onwards) carried it through dozens of editions to 1651.
literary_significance: The most widely read English wisdom-book of the early modern period and a key channel by which classical moral philosophy reached vernacular readers; it established Baldwin's reputation before his editorship of A Mirror for Magistrates.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1547 (STC 1253); later editions enlarged by Thomas Palfreyman. Facsimile of the 1620 edition: Scholars' Facsimiles & Reprints, 1975.

title: Beware the Cat
alternative_titles: Beware the Cat: The First English Novel
description: William Baldwin's anti-Catholic prose satire of 1552–53, in which a company of men swap stories proving that cats can speak and understand; printed posthumously in 1561 and often claimed as the first English novel.
plot_or_argument: The narrator, Master Streamer, overhears a conversation among the household of John Young while lodged at the printing house; the talk turns to cats, and Gregory Streamer relates how, having eaten a cat, he gained the power to understand animal speech, recounting the trial of Mouse-slayer before the cat parliament and the bawdy doings of cats and priests — a satire on Catholic superstition, oral tradition, and the credulity of tale-collectors.
narrative_structure: A framed narrative in three orations, with inset stories (the cat's life of Grimalkin, the trial of Mouse-slayer) and a self-conscious apparatus of marginal glosses and running commentary on the reliability of oral report.
principal_characters: Master Streamer (narrator); Gregory Streamer; Mouse-slayer; Grimalkin; John Young (the printer)
historical_context: Written in 1552–53 at the press of John Day, where Baldwin worked; its satire of Catholic ritual (the cat's mass) fitted the Edwardian Reformation moment, and by its printing in 1561 (with a prefatory epistle to John Young) the political climate had changed again.
literary_significance: Claimed as the first English novel for its sustained prose fiction and self-conscious narrative framing; it is also a sophisticated satire on storytelling, tradition, and the authority of print, anticipating the narrative experiments of the Elizabethan period.
attribution_notes: Printed anonymously in 1561 with initials 'G. B.'; the attribution to William Baldwin rests on the prefatory matter and the internal evidence of the printing-house setting, and is accepted by modern scholarship.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1561 (STC 1245); standard edition: Beware the Cat: The First English Novel, ed. William A. Ringler, Jr., and Michael Flachmann (Huntington Library, 1988).

title: The Itinerary
description: John Leland's topographical survey of England and Wales, the record of his itineraries undertaken with a royal commission from Henry VIII to search the libraries of the monasteries, compiled c. 1535–43 and first printed by Thomas Hearne in 1710–12.
plot_or_argument: The Itinerary is a county-by-county record of Leland's travels: towns, rivers, bridges, castles, churches, and the antiquities of each place, noted in terse first-person entries that document the landscape of England on the eve of the dissolution of the monasteries.
narrative_structure: Topographical notes arranged by county, preserved in autograph notebooks; the printed text of 1710–12 follows Hearne's edition of the surviving manuscripts.
historical_context: Leland held a commission from Henry VIII (1533) to search the monastic and collegiate libraries; his itineraries of c. 1535–43 covered most of England and Wales, and his notes preserve records of books, inscriptions, and buildings later destroyed in the dissolution and after.
literary_significance: The founding text of English antiquarianism and topography; it inaugurated the tradition of the county survey that runs through Camden, Aubrey, and the eighteenth-century antiquaries, and its value as an eyewitness record of pre-dissolution England is irreplaceable.
bibliographical_notes: First printed by Thomas Hearne, 9 vols, 1710–12 (2nd ed. 1744–45); standard edition: The Itinerary of John Leland, ed. Lucy Toulmin Smith, 5 vols (1906–10; repr. 1964).

title: Cygnea Cantio
description: Leland's Latin poem in praise of the Thames, in which a swan sings as it glides down the river from Oxford to London, celebrating the towns, palaces, and worthies along its banks; published with a long commentary by the author in 1545.
plot_or_argument: The swan's song follows the Thames from its source past Oxford, Windsor, and Hampton Court to Westminster and London, praising each place and the Tudor dynasty; the commentary supplies the antiquarian and topographical learning that the verse compresses.
narrative_structure: A single long Latin poem with Leland's own prose commentary, a form modelled on the Renaissance edition of a classical text.
historical_context: Published 1545 during Leland's final productive years, as part of his programme of celebrating the antiquities of Britain in Latin verse (the unpublished Genethliacon and the unfinished De uiris illustribus).
literary_significance: The earliest sustained literary celebration of the Thames and the model for the river-poems of Spenser (the Thames–Medway marriage) and Denham's Cooper's Hill; a key monument of Tudor antiquarian humanism.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1545 (STC 15446); modern edition: John Leland: De uiris illustribus / On Famous Men, ed. James P. Carley (PIMS/British Library, 2010) includes discussion; text of Cygnea Cantio with translation in Carley, 'John Leland in Paris', and in Leland's Itinerary, ed. Toulmin Smith, vol. 5.

title: The New Chronicles of England and France
description: Robert Fabyan's chronicle of England and France from Brutus to the reign of Henry VII, compiled from the London chronicles and printed by Richard Pynson in 1516 as The New Chronicles of England and France; the first city chronicle of London to reach print.
plot_or_argument: The chronicle narrates the kings of England (with a parallel account of France) reign by reign, drawn from the Brut, the London chronicles, and the work of the French chroniclers, and closes with the accession of Henry VIII; the appended 'Concordance of Histories' aligns the chronicles of England and France.
narrative_structure: Annalistic chronicle in seven parts, each divided by reign; Fabyan's additions include the civic history of London and verse 'Lenvoyes' moralizing each reign.
historical_context: Compiled by Fabyan, a London draper and alderman, from the 1490s to c. 1504, with continuations to 1516; printed by Pynson in 1516 and again by William Rastell in 1533, it supplied material to Hall, Holinshed, and the Elizabethan playwrights.
literary_significance: The first printed London chronicle and a major conduit of the English historical tradition from the medieval Brut to the Tudor chroniclers; Shakespeare knew its material (including the story of Lear) through Holinshed and the chronicle tradition.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1516 (STC 10659); modern edition: The New Chronicles of England and France, ed. Henry Ellis (1811).

title: The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York
alternative_titles: The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancastre and Yorke
description: Edward Hall's chronicle of the Wars of the Roses and the triumph of the house of Tudor, from the deposition of Richard II to the death of Henry VIII; printed posthumously by Richard Grafton in 1548 and continued by Grafton in later editions.
plot_or_argument: Hall narrates the dynastic strife between Lancaster and York as a providential drama culminating in the union of the two houses in Henry VIII, with long set-piece speeches and a moralizing emphasis on the ruin brought by ambition, faction, and rebellion; the reign of Henry VIII occupies the final section ('The Triumphant Reign of King Henry the VIII').
narrative_structure: Chronicle divided by reigns, from Richard II through Henry VIII, framed by a preface on the theme of union and enriched with speeches invented in the manner of classical historiography.
principal_characters: Henry IV; Henry V; Henry VI; Edward IV; Richard III; Henry VII; Henry VIII; Cardinal Wolsey
historical_context: Compiled over the 1530s and 1540s by Hall, a lawyer and MP, drawing on More's Richard III, Polydore Vergil, and Fabyan; the 1548 edition was supervised by Grafton, who added continuations in the editions of 1550.
literary_significance: The principal source of Shakespeare's English history plays (the second tetralogy follows Hall closely) and the classic statement of the Tudor myth of union and providential kingship; its dramatic speeches made it the most literary of the Tudor chronicles.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1548 (STC 12721); modern reprint: Hall's Chronicle, ed. Henry Ellis (1809; repr. AMS, 1965).

title: The Seven Penitential Psalms (Fisher's exposition)
alternative_titles: This treatise concerninge the fruytfull saynges of Davyd the kynge and prophete in the seven penytencyall psalmes
description: John Fisher's devotional exposition of the seven penitential psalms, preached as sermons to Margaret Beaufort and published by Wynkyn de Worde in 1508; the first work of the English Catholic humanist reform tradition.
plot_or_argument: The treatise expounds Psalms 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, and 143 as a programme of penitence — contrition, confession, and satisfaction — applying each psalm to the life of the Christian penitent and to the passion of Christ as the ground of forgiveness.
narrative_structure: Seven sermon-treatises, one per psalm, each structured by the threefold division of the penitential process, with a preface to Margaret Beaufort.
historical_context: Preached as a Lenten course to the household of Lady Margaret Beaufort, the king's mother, whose confessor Fisher was; printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1508 and reprinted in 1509 and 1525, it belongs to the devotional revival associated with the Charterhouse and the early humanist circle.
literary_significance: The finest English devotional prose before the Reformation controversy and a witness to the scriptural piety of the pre-Reformation English Church; its emphasis on preaching and scripture anticipates the reform movements on both sides of the sixteenth-century divide.
bibliographical_notes: First printed by Wynkyn de Worde, 1508 (STC 10902); modern edition: The English Works of John Fisher, Part I, ed. John E. B. Mayor (EETS e.s. 27, 1876).

title: Lily's Grammar
description: The authorized Latin grammar of the English schools, compiled from the grammars of William Lily and John Colet, edited and revised by Erasmus, and imposed by royal proclamation of Henry VIII in 1540 as the single grammar to be used in all schools.
plot_or_argument: A textbook in two parts: the English 'Introduction of the Eight Parts of Speech' (the Accidence) and the Latin 'Brevissima Institutio' (syntax and prosody), with the famous prefatory poem 'Carmen de Moribus' on schoolboy manners.
narrative_structure: Two-part pedagogical manual, with rules, paradigms, and examples arranged for memorization.
historical_context: The grammar grew out of Colet's statutes for St Paul's School (c. 1509), Lily's part in its composition, and Erasmus's revisions; after Lily's death (1522) it was printed in various forms until the royal proclamation of 1540 and the authorized edition of 1549 standardized it, making it the one book every grammar-school boy knew.
literary_significance: The most influential textbook in the history of English education: in use (as the 'Eton Grammar') for three centuries, it shaped the Latinity of every educated English writer from Shakespeare to Johnson, and its jingling rules became proverbial.
attribution_notes: A collaborative compilation traditionally credited to William Lily as first high master of St Paul's; Colet and Erasmus contributed substantially, and the standard attribution to Lily is conventional rather than strictly authorial.
bibliographical_notes: Authorized edition 1549 (STC 15611); modern facsimile: A Shorte Introduction of Grammar (1549), ed. Vincent J. Flynn (Scholars' Facsimiles & Reprints, 1945).

title: Aeditio
description: The elementary Latin grammar composed for St Paul's School, traditionally attributed to John Colet with the collaboration of William Lily and Erasmus; the English 'Accidence' later incorporated into the authorized Lily's Grammar.
plot_or_argument: A short accidence of the eight parts of speech with English rules and Latin examples, designed for beginners at St Paul's, prefaced by Colet's school statutes and the 'Carmen de Moribus'.
narrative_structure: Pedagogical manual with rules and paradigms.
historical_context: Composed c. 1509–18 for the school Colet founded in 1509 and refounded in 1512 with Mercers' Company endowment; the English Accidence printed as Aeditio in 1527 became the basis of the royal grammar of 1540.
literary_significance: The germ of the national school grammar and a document of the Erasmian educational reform at its English source, St Paul's School.
attribution_notes: The grammar is a collaborative production of the St Paul's circle; the traditional ascription to Colet as founder reflects the school's origin rather than sole authorship, and Erasmus revised the text.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1527 (STC 5542); modern study: J. H. Lupton, A Life of John Colet (1887); text of the Carmen de Moribus in Lily's Grammar editions.

title: De Emendata Structura Latini Sermonis
alternative_titles: On the Correct Structure of Latin Prose
description: Thomas Linacre's treatise on Latin syntax, published in London by Richard Pynson in 1524; the first systematic Latin grammar composed by an Englishman and a landmark of the humanist reform of grammar.
plot_or_argument: The work analyses Latin construction in six books, replacing the medieval speculative grammars with a descriptive account of syntax based on the usage of Cicero and the best classical authors, illustrated with abundant quotations.
narrative_structure: Six books of systematic grammatical exposition with a preface to Prince Arthur's tutor and a dedication to the grammar-school masters.
historical_context: Linacre, physician to Henry VIII and the foremost English Greek scholar of his generation, composed the work over 1512–24 after his return from Italy; it was printed by Pynson and used in the schools alongside the authorized grammar.
literary_significance: A founding document of English classical scholarship; its descriptive method influenced the whole European tradition of Latin grammar, and it secured Linacre's European reputation among humanists.
bibliographical_notes: First edition: London, Richard Pynson, 1524 (STC 15634); continental editions at Paris (1527) and Basel (1555); no complete modern edition; standard study: F. J. Norton, 'Thomas Linacre and the printing of the De Emendata Structura', and C. G. Allen's work on Linacre's library.

title: Linacre's Galen translations
alternative_titles: The Galen Translations of Thomas Linacre
description: Thomas Linacre's Latin translations of six treatises of Galen, printed by Richard Pynson between 1521 and 1523, which restored the Greek Galen to European medicine and established Linacre as the founder of the English school of medical humanism.
plot_or_argument: The translations cover Galen's De sanitate tuenda, Methodus medendi, De temperamentis, De naturalibus facultatibus, De pulsuum usu, and De symptomatum differentiis, rendered into a purified humanist Latin from the Greek texts Linacre collated.
narrative_structure: Six separate treatises translated and printed with prefaces to Henry VIII and to Linacre's medical colleagues.
historical_context: Translated c. 1517–23 after Linacre's Greek studies under Chalcondyles and Politian in Italy; Pynson printed the treatises in 1521–23, and they were reprinted on the continent, remaining the standard Latin Galen for over a century.
literary_significance: The founding texts of English medical humanism: by purging the medieval Latin Galen of Arabist corruption, Linacre transformed European medical education and helped found the Royal College of Physicians (1518), of which he was first president.
bibliographical_notes: First editions: London, Richard Pynson, 1521–23 (STC 11535–11539); modern reprints in the Opera of 1550 and later continental editions; standard study: C. D. O'Malley, 'English Medical Humanists: Thomas Linacre and John Caius' (1965).

title: The Pastime of People
alternative_titles: The Pastyme of People: The Cronycles of Dyuers Realmys
description: John Rastell's chronicle of the kings of England, printed by the author c. 1529 and known principally through the celebrated woodcut portraits of the kings that illustrate it.
plot_or_argument: The chronicle surveys the kings of Britain from the legendary line (Brutus, Arthur) through the Saxon, Norman, and Plantagenet reigns to the author's own day, each reign summarized with a woodcut portrait, the whole prefaced by a prologue on the use of history.
narrative_structure: A compressed annalistic chronicle with full-page woodcut portraits of the kings, arranged by reign.
historical_context: Printed c. 1529 by Rastell, More's brother-in-law, printer, and playwright, at his own press; only three copies survive, and the king-portraits became a standard visual source for the Tudor image of English kingship.
literary_significance: A pioneering illustrated chronicle whose woodcut royal portraits influenced the visual tradition of the English kings for centuries; it documents the early Tudor printing industry's combination of history and spectacle.
bibliographical_notes: First edition c. 1529 (STC 20724); facsimile edition by T. F. Dibdin (1811); standard study: E. J. Devereux, A Bibliography of John Rastell (1999).

title: The Introduction of Knowledge
alternative_titles: The Fyrst Boke of the Introduction of Knowledge
description: Andrew Boorde's popular geography and travel book of 1547, the first English printed book to describe the nations of Europe in verse and prose for the general reader.
plot_or_argument: The book presents each nation of Europe (and beyond) through a woodcut portrait of a native in national dress, a verse dialogue spoken by the figure, and a prose description of the country's customs, currency, and distances — a compendium of travel knowledge for merchants and pilgrims.
narrative_structure: Thirty-nine chapters, one per nation, each combining woodcut, verse self-description, and prose itinerary.
historical_context: Compiled from Boorde's European travels of the 1530s and printed in 1547 by William Copland; Boorde, physician and Carthusian, had been licensed to travel by Thomas Cromwell, and the book reflects the expansion of English geographical curiosity in the mid-Tudor period.
literary_significance: The first printed English survey of European nations and an early document of English ethnographic description; its woodcut national portraits founded a visual tradition that lasted into the seventeenth century.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1547 (STC 3382); facsimile edition: ed. F. J. Furnivall (EETS e.s. 10, 1870).

title: The Dyetary of Health
alternative_titles: A Compendyous Regyment or a Dyetary of Helth
description: Andrew Boorde's vernacular regimen of health, first printed in 1542; a popular handbook of diet, dwelling, and daily conduct for the English householder.
plot_or_argument: The book advises on diet (meats, drinks, bread, and their digestions), on choosing a healthy dwelling site, on sleep and clothing, and on the management of the body's humours, in a plain and often earthy prose salted with proverbs and personal opinion.
narrative_structure: A systematic handbook in short chapters, arranged by topic from dwelling-place to foodstuffs to regimen.
historical_context: Written by Boorde after his return from his European travels and printed in 1542 (with many later editions to 1630); it belongs to the same vernacular medical movement as Elyot's Castle of Health, aimed at readers without Latin.
literary_significance: One of the most popular health manuals of the sixteenth century and a rich source for Tudor domestic life, diet, and popular medicine; Boorde's colloquial style anticipates the plain-speaking of later popular medical writing.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1542 (STC 3378); modern edition: The Dyetary of Health, ed. F. J. Furnivall (EETS e.s. 10, 1870).

title: Vulgaria
description: Robert Whittington's collection of everyday sentences in English with their Latin renderings, printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1520; the most celebrated of the Tudor vulgaria used to teach Latin composition by translation.
plot_or_argument: The book presents model English sentences — the talk of the schoolroom, the market, and the household — each with its idiomatic Latin equivalent, arranged to drill the schoolboy in the idiom of daily speech turned into classical Latin.
narrative_structure: A collection of sentence-pairs grouped by topic, prefaced by Whittington's remarks on teaching method.
historical_context: Printed in 1520 at the height of the grammar-school humanist reform; Whittington, a prolific grammarian and laureate of Oxford, was among the schoolmasters who replaced the medieval grammars with humanist vulgaria, and his book was reprinted through the 1520s.
literary_significance: The finest surviving example of the Tudor vulgarium and a vivid record of early sixteenth-century English speech and schoolroom practice; it documents the humanist method of teaching Latin through the vernacular.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1520 (STC 25577); modern edition: The Vulgaria of John Stanbridge and the Vulgaria of Robert Whittinton, ed. Beatrice White (EETS o.s. 187, 1932).
